entities.name: Gonzalo de Sandoval
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gonzalo de Sandoval was a Spanish conquistador who played a pivotal role in the early colonization of New Spain (Mexico) in the early 16th century. He was a key figure in the expedition led by Hernán Cortés, serving as a trusted lieutenant and co-governor of the colony while Cortés was away from the capital.

De Sandoval's significance lies in his role as a bridge between the indigenous peoples of Mexico and the Spanish colonizers, as well as his involvement in the defeat of the Aztec Empire. His legacy can be seen in the establishment of Spanish rule in Mexico, which had a profound impact on the region's politics, culture, and economy.

Despite his importance in the conquest of Mexico, de Sandoval's life was marked by personal struggles and conflicts. He was accused of treason and faced exile, but ultimately returned to Mexico and continued to play a significant role in the colony's affairs.

Today, de Sandoval is remembered as a complex and multifaceted figure, whose actions and decisions had far-reaching consequences for the indigenous peoples of Mexico and the Spanish Empire as a whole.
